Single-phase M-type barium hexaferrite (BaFe12O19) nanocrystals were synthesized using a modified flux method.
Nanocrystals initially spherical (~7-10 nm) transformed to prism-shaped (~20-40 nm) after annealing.
Microwave annealing (MWA) was conducted at powers from 160 to 760 watts for 5 minutes.
Vacuum annealing (VA) was performed at temperatures from 200 to 1200 °C for 4 hours.
MWA increased particle size modestly from 7.3 to 13.4 nm, while VA increased it substantially to 40.4 nm.
Maximum reflection loss (RL) of 37.15 dB at 16 GHz was achieved with MWA at 760 watt.
Maximum RL of 27.56 dB at 15.75 GHz was achieved with VA at 1200 °C.
RL measurements were done on 2 mm thick coatings in the Ku-band (12.4-18.0 GHz).
TEM and SAED confirmed the hexagonal BaFe12O19 phase and morphological evolution.
XRD patterns showed increased peak intensities with annealing but less particle growth in MWA compared to VA.
Ostwald ripening explains the growth of larger crystals at the expense of smaller ones during annealing.
Quantum size effect causes discrete electronic energy levels that enhance microwave absorption.
MWA produces faster morphological transformation than VA due to higher diffusion rates in molten NaCl flux.
The aspect ratio (length/breadth) of fully grown nanocrystals ranged from 2 to 6.
Magnetic properties and RL increased systematically with increasing annealing power or temperature.
The modified flux method involves coating precipitated powder with NaCl in a 1:2 weight ratio.
Annealed samples exhibited superlattice reflections in electron diffraction patterns.
MWA favors electron movement inside particles, enhancing crystallinity without large particle growth.
VA favors atomic diffusion, leading to larger particle growth but slower crystallization.
Accurate EM impedance matching and multipolarization contribute to excellent microwave absorption.
